description: Erect or decumbent, suffrutescent, few-stemmed, 10-30 cm high. Stems herbaceous to woody, up to 25 cm long, 1-2 mm in diam., pubescent with curved hairs, rarely also with scattered long erect hairs, with stalked and sessile glands. Leaves: Lower alternate, upper opposite, those of a pair unequal. the smaller leaves with lateral branches and/or inflorescences in the axil; petiole with the same indumentum as the stem, 0.2-0.5 x as long as the blade, 5-20 mm long, sometimes geniculate at the apex, not flattened at the base; stipules subulate or acicular, 4-14 mm long, reddish, with the same indumentum and glands as the stem or with only rather long hairs; blade simple, narrowly elliptic to elliptic at the base of the stems, elsewhere on the plant narrowly ovate to very narrowly ovate, 2-9 x as long as wide, 15-70 x 5-15 mm, obtuse or acute, mucronate at the apex, truncate to cuneate at the base, at the basal ¼-½ entire or rarely obscurely serrate, at the terminal part serrate at the margin, granulose on both sides, with sessile glands, sparsely to moderately pubescent or velutinous, the hairs on the veins beneath more conspicuous and more numerous, and mostly with stalked glands; main veins subpinnate, 3 branching from the base, impressed above, prominent beneath. Inflorescences axillary or terminal, 1-3-flowered, 60-120 mm long. Peduncles and pedicels slender, with the same indumentum as the stem and, furthermore, with the stalked glands conspicuous; peduncles 0.5-2(5) x as long as the pedicels, 15-55 mm long; pedicels 9-50 mm long and geniculate under the fruit; involucral bracts usually 3 per flower, conspicuous, sepal-like, 5-15 mm long. Sepals green to blackish, free, narrowly ovate to ovate, or narrowly obovate to obovate, 2-3.5 x as long as wide, 10-15 x 4-5 mm, outside pubescent or obscurely pubescent, with curved hairs, and with numerous long stalked glands, inside glabrous, with 3 parallel main veins; mucro terete, 1-4 mm long, reddish to purplish, with the same indumentum as the sepal and furthermore, also with a few scattered long erect hairs, with a small tuft of downy hairs or rarely with a pocket of yellowish resinous granules at the base. Petals obtriangular, 1-2 x as long as wide, 15-30 x 10-25 mm, 1.3-2.5 x as long as the sepals, 1.5-3 x as long as the stamens, pink or mauve, with 5 or mostly 7 purplish main veins, outside glabrous or with scattered, shortly stalked glands, inside pilose, puberulent and auriculate at the base, ciliate in the basal half at the margin, obscurely sinuate to crenate at the apex. Stamens (rarely some imperfect), monadelphous; groups basally connate for 1-2 mm; filaments of each group basally connate for 2-3 mm; filaments in the central stamens 8-9 mm and in the lateral 6-7 mm long, terete and apically recurved, hairy outside, glabrous inside; an ovate rimmed gland-cavity is situated on the outer side of the base of each group; anthers oblong, those of the long filaments sometimes slightly larger, 2.5-3.5 x 1-1.2 mm, rarely sterile and then 1.4 x 0.5 mm, normally shaped or deformed, subintrorse. Pistil 10-15 mm long; ovary obovoid, 2-3 x 2 mm, hyalino-pubescent or hirto-pubescent; beak longitudinally grooved, 4-8 mm long, pubescent, mostly with numerous stalked glands; style when present 0.5-1 mm long, obscurely hairy; stigmas linear to clavate, 3-4 x 0.4-0.6 mm, outer side obscurely hairy, margin subentire to crenate, apex obtuse or acute. Fruit 45 mm long; mericarps 11 x 2 mm and beak 35 mm long; mericarps hirsute, obliquely rimmed and ridged at the apex; beak hirsute outside, hispid inside where the tail detaches from the beak-axis; these stiff hairs copper-coloured and long at the tail's base, forming a crest. Seed narrowly obovoid, 4 mm long, glabrous.

description: Glabrescent stem parasite to 1 m. Leaves subsessile, elliptic-lanceolate. Flowers in axillary umbels, glabrous, tubular with a basal swelling, 5-lobed, mostly orange but red below and with a black tip. Shrubs perhaps 1 m high, essentially glabrous. Leaves alternate, subopposite, occasionally fascicled, somewhat coriaceous with age, mostly elliptic-linear to lanceolate (greatly variable in size), (15-)30-40(-80) x 5-10 mm; petioles 2-4 mm long. Inflorescence a 3-6-flowered umbel, or occasionally racemose by the addition of several flowers lower on the rachis, axillary or solitary on older stems. Flowers 5-merous; mature buds 30-40 mm long, orange basally, yellow above, the apical portion blackish, mostly cylindrical but slightly expanded basally. Corolla gamopetalous, bilaterally symmetrical (the tube bearing a short, 'V'-shaped, unilateral split), lobes slightly longer than rest of corolla and spirally coiled at anthesis. Filaments attached near base of lobes, anthers normally breaking from filament at anthesis (the flower opens explosively). Style filiform; stigma capitate. Aerial, hemiparasitic shrub, up to 1 m high, essentially glabrous. Leaves alternate, opposite- subopposite, occasionally fascicled, somewhat coriaceous with age, linear-lanceolate to narrowly elliptic, glabrous, obscurely nerved, lower ones strongly ascending. Inflorescence a 4-6-flowered umbel, or occasionally racemose by addition of several flowers lower on rachis, axillary or solitary on older branches. Flowers 5-merous, tubular, bilaterally symmetrical (tube bearing a short, V-shaped, unilateral split), bright red to orange basally, yellow towards tip, apical portion blackish, mostly cylindrical but slightly expanded basally; lobes slightly longer than rest of corolla, spirally coiled following anthesis. Flowering time Apr.-Aug. Fruit an ellipsoid berry, reddish when mature, smooth. Glabrescent stem parasite, up to 1 m tall. Leaves elliptic-lanceolate. Flowers 76-152 mm axillary umbels, tubular, base swollen, mouth V-shaped, 5 lobes coiling back, glabrous, orange-red and black-tipped. Berry red.

description: Perennial herb, geophyte, 0.3-0.5 m high; corm tunics of brown fibres; stem erect, simple or with 1 or 2 branches. Leaf 1, linear, canaliculate, usually dry and broken distally. Spathes herbaceous, apex dry, brown. Inflorescence with white to cream-coloured flowers; nectar guides yellow, with dark spots at edges; tepals unequal, outer 30-35 mm long, spreading horizontally, claw strongly ascending, inner 5-7 mm long, cusp-like, sometimes 3-lobed apically, acute. Stamens: filaments 7-8 mm long, united in cylindric column, free apically for ± 0.5 mm; anthers 5-6 mm long; pollen white. Ovary ± cylindric, ± 10 mm long; style branches up to 7 mm long; crests slender, up to 8 mm long. Flowering time Dec.-Mar. Plants 400-600 mm high, often with fibrous collar around base. Corm 14-20 mm diam.; tunics of brown fibres. Stem simple or 1- or 2-branched, sheathing leaves 3 or 4, with dry brown, attenuate apices, 40-60 mm long. Foliage leaf solitary, basal, channelled, linear, exceeding stem, often dry and broken distally. Rhipidial spathes with dry, brown, attenuate apices, inner 50-70 mm long, outer ± 2/3 as long. Flowers long-lived, white to creamy yellow, outer tepal limbs with narrow, deep yellow nectar guides at bases, spreading or laxly reflexed; outer tepals 30-35 x ± 15 mm, limb 15-20 mm long, claws as long to slightly shorter, darkly speckled, smooth; inner tepals vestigial, 5-7 mm long, hair-like, sometimes obscurely 3-lobed distally. Filaments ± 7 mm long, united below, free and diverging in upper 1 mm; anthers 5-6 mm, white; pollen white. Ovary ± cylindric, 7-9 mm long; style branches ± 7 mm long, crests ± linear, 7-8 mm long. Capsules and seeds unknown.

description: The only blue-flowered member of subg. Grandiflorae in southern Africa, Moraea ardesiaca is immediately recognised by the large flowers either slate-blue to blue-mauve. Confusion with M. carnea is possible but this species has pale pink flowers with darker pink to purple style crests and smaller, narrower tepals 55-60 mm long vs. 65-70 mm in M. ardesiaca. Moraea carnea also occurs along streams on open slopes at relatively high elevations, usually above 2300 m, whereas M. ardesiaca is generally found at lower elevations along streams and drainage lines.

description: Plants 500-700 mm high, usually solitary. Corm ± 15 mm diam.; tunics of medium-textured, netted fibres. Stem sheathed below by light brown, broken cataphylls, unbranched, partly covered by sheathing leaves 2(3), ± 100 mm long, lower part often exposed. Foliage leaf linear, channelled, usually exceeding stem, 5-10(-25) mm wide. Rhipidial spathes grey-green with light brown tips, inner 90-140 mm long, outer ± 2/3 as long. description: Coastal populations of M. bulbillifera are unmistakable for the strongly cormiferous habit, but even plants lacking cormlets in the aerial axils are fairly easy to distinguish from other solitary-leaved species by their flowers with the narrow tepal cup enclosing only the filaments, with the anthers and well-developed style branches and crests extending well above the cup. The foliage leaf is usually inserted at or very close to the ground but plants from the drier valleys at the northern edge of its range are often confusing as the leaf may be inserted rather high above ground. Two subspecies are recognised. The typical subsp. bulbillifera is coastal and always found on sandy or limestone substrates. It is usually robust and has a well-developed cormiferous habit. Subsp. anomala occurs inland, mainly in renosterveld, on the rolling clay plains of the southern Cape, extending into the sandy and rocky valleys of the Langeberg and Riviersonderend Mtns. Sometimes as robust as subsp. bulbillifera, it is more often a much smaller plant, especially in drier habitats, with the dwarfing extending to the flowers as well.

description: Large-flowered Moraea comptonii is distinguished by the fiddle-shaped to spathulate tepals weakly divided into claw and limb, with the lower halves forming an open cup and upper halves spreading. The flowers are particularly strongly and sweetly scented and either entirely yellow, or salmon-pink to orange with a yellow cup, often with dark green markings in the lower third. Like its close relative M. elegans, plants have a solitary leaf, a partly to fully included ovary, and the inner rhipidial spathes become enlarged to enclose the developing capsules. Also like M. elegans, the filaments are fully united in a column tapering from a wide base but the anthers are usually shorter than the style branches in contrast to M. elegans, in which the anthers exceed the style branches. Another difference between the two is that the tepals of M. elegans are more-or-less ovate, widest in the lower third, and the tepal markings are confined to the outer tepals in the upper third, whereas tepals of M. comptonii are widest in the distal third and are either unmarked or have markings at the bases of the tepal limbs of both whorls.

description: Closely allied to Moraea tripetala, M. cuspidata is distinguished by the linear inner tepals up to 15 mm long (rarely less than 10 mm), spreading in the distal half, and usually with a particularly narrow foliage leaf with the halves usually tightly appressed in dry conditions. The brown to almost black corm tunics consist of thickened vertical fibres sometimes with raised ridges, and form a collar of stiff fibres around the base of the stem. The flowers are pale blue to violet with the large, velvety nectar guides spotted with dark blue on a white background. The filaments are usually united for 1.0-1.5 mm but occasionally less, and are ± as long as or slightly shorter than the dark purple anthers that bear red pollen. Capsules (where known) are relatively large, 14-16 mm long and the seeds are also relatively large, 1.8-2.0 mm long and unusual in having a pale, spongy testa much thickened into prominent ridges on the angles. The species is sympatric at some sites and even co-blooming with smaller-flowered Moraea amabilis (also allied to M. tripetala) but that species has a broadly channelled foliage leaf, sometimes plane distally and often pilose on the abaxial surface, and consistently short, hair-like inner tepals typically 1.5-2.0 mm long. At sites where they have been recorded growing together pollen of M. amabilis is white, contrasting with the orange-red pollen of M. cuspidata. An outlying record of M. cuspidata from Perdekloof, southeast of Oudtshoorn, probably belongs here. The flowers are exceptionally small, the inner tepals are 8-9 mm long, otherwise consistent with the species.

description: Plants small, 70-200 mm high. Corm 5-10 mm diam.; tunics of black or brown, wiry or ± soft-textured fibres. description: Distinguished by the large flowers with predominantly yellow tepals spreading from the base, the tepals oblong and broadest in the lower half with the outer tepals strikingly marked with large green or green and orange blotches in the distal half. Plants have a solitary foliage leaf and bear few to several branches. The anthers, 8-10 mm long, are borne on a sturdy filament column wide at the base and tapering to a narrow apex, and exceed the style branches, an important distinction between M. elegans and closely allied M. comptonii, which has shorter anthers, either uniformly yellow or salmon to orange flowers with a yellow cup with or without green markings, these at the base of the spathulate or fiddle-shaped outer tepals, thus in the middle to lower third of the tepals. Moraea elegans and M. comptonii have complementary ranges in the Caledon and Bredasdorp Districts and are generally easy to distinguish, although some populations of M. comptonii approach M. elegans in appearance.

description: Recognised by the flexuose stem, sharply flexed above the sheaths of the two to four leaves, the lowermost of these inserted well above ground level. All nodes of the stem bear foliage leaves except for the terminal which bears the inflorescence. The pink (rarely yellow) flowers have a yellow cup formed by the diverging tepals claws, often so narrow at the base that the edges are gapped, the cup thus windowed near the base. Plants from the Koedoes Mtns lack these windows but in other respects match the type except that some plants have uniformly yellow flowers. The flowers have filaments united in a slender column, only slightly wider toward the base, and contiguous anthers, with the stigmatic tips of the forked style branches extending between the anthers.

description: Closely resembling Moraea fugax in general appearance except smaller in all features, M. filicaulis has a slender, almost filiform stem ± 1 mm in diam., and one or more often two subequal or unequal, filiform, narrowly channelled leaves inserted at the first above ground internode. The flowers are usually white, but occasionally pink or blue-mauve or even violet, and have outer tepals mostly 20-35 mm long (occasionally longer) and inner tepals 18-30 mm long. Flowers of M. fugax have outer tepals mostly 30-45 mm long and inner tepals 25-35 mm long. The inner rhipidial spathes, a useful measure of plant size, are 20-35(-40) mm long in M. filicaulis but 40-65 mm long in M. fugax. Moraea filicaulis has been treated as a subspecies of M. fugax and an important reason for recognising it as a separate species is that it sometimes co-occurs with typical M. fugax but always showing slightly different habitat preferences.

description: Distinguished by its robust, several- to many-branched stem and characteristic flowers with the tepal claws widely diverging to form a shallow dish including the filaments and bases of the anthers. The tepals are usually salmon-pink with a yellow cup but populations with uniformly yellow flowers are not uncommon. When dry the shape of the flowers is often lost but its large size makes identification fairly easy. The tepals, ovary, filaments, anthers, and capsules are amongst the largest in the genus. The outer tepals are usually 35-40 mm long, and the filaments are ± 8 mm long with the anthers up to 11 mm long. The ovary, initially 17-20 mm long, elongates after fertilization and the capsules may reach a length of 55 mm. The capsules are notable in having a pointed beak some 2 mm long. Earlier-flowering Moraea collina has been confused in the past with M. flaccida but is a shorter, few-branched species, the flowers with suberect tepal claws forming a narrow cup enclosing both filaments and anthers. The tepals of M. collina seldom exceed 35 mm, the filaments are 6-7 mm long, and the anthers are slightly shorter, 5?6 mm long. The ovary in M. collina is often as long as that of M. flaccida and the capsule may attain a length of over 35 mm. Capsules of M. collina, however, have a shorter, rather obtuse beak ± 1 mm long. Although M. flaccida flowers relatively late in the season, by which time M. collina is usually in fruit, their flowering times may overlap and natural hybrids have been recorded between the two species on the Cape Peninsula.

description: So unusual is Moraea flexicaulis that when first described it was assigned to a separate sect. Flexuosae of subg. Moraea, but molecular studies have shown it to be deeply nested in subg. Homeria, in which its chromosome number, 2n = 12, and karyotype of exclusively acrocentric chromosomes are consistent, as are the largely united filaments forming a sturdy, cylindric column. Moraea flexicaulis is now considered to be most closely allied to two Namaqualand species of subg. Homeria, M. schlechteri and M. knersvlaktensis, all three with several leaves, even those in the upper part of the stem with free blades, and filaments free and diverging distally. The species remains a very distinctive member of the subgenus. Its particularly well-developed style branches and crests are exceptional in subg. Homeria but both its presumed close allies have style branches bearing moderately well-developed crests although they have much shorter style branches. Blooming early in the season, in late June and July, Moraea flexicaulis comes into flower three to four weeks after the first soaking autumn or winter rains fall in this arid area of the southern African northwest coast. As with many plants of arid areas, plant size is very variable depending on rainfall. Plants from the base of the Ploegberg in the Richtersveld are unusually robust compared to other collections, up to 150 mm tall (vs. < 100 mm elsewhere) and with larger rhipidial spathes (45-50 mm vs. 20-40 mm) and broader leaves, leaving open the possibility that they may be a separate species but this remains uncertain until more material is available.

description: Cormous geophyte, up to 150 mm tall, branched. Leaves 2 or 3, linear, fairly short, channelled. Flowers enclosed in green spathes, yellow, tepal claws long, limbs shorter, outspread, filaments united in a slender column, style branches narrow, diverging, crests short, erect. Plants 60-150 mm high. Corm 10-15 mm diam.; tunics of matted, relatively fine, dark brown (± black) fibres. Stem flexuose, flexed above sheathing base of each leaf, with up to 4 branches, rarely simple, without sheathing leaves. Foliage leaves 3 to 5, lowermost inserted shortly (up to 20 mm) above ground and largest, upper leaves progressively shorter, falcate, channelled, up to 60 mm long, 3-6 mm wide. Rhipidial spathes ± attenuate, with dry apices, inner 25-50 mm long, outer mostly ± 1/2 as long, free and arching outward in distal 2/3. Flowers fugaceous, pale yellow, limbs of all tepals with deeper yellow nectar guides at bases, spreading horizontally, outer tepal guides sometimes with numerous small dark green dots or clear yellow, faintly scented; outer tepals narrowly lanceolate, 28-30 x ± 8 mm, claws ± erect, ± 14 mm long, inner tepals 25-27 x 7 mm long, claws narrow ± as long as limbs, limbs twisted through 45º. Filaments 11-12 mm long, united in a cylindric column, free in upper ± 1.5 mm and diverging; anthers straight, ± 3.5 mm long, white; pollen white. Ovary ± 7 mm long, ± cylindric, flushed red; style branches 4 mm long, crests ± 2 mm long, erect. Capsules ovoid, 12-15 mm long. Seeds obovoid, ± smooth.

description: Distinguished primarily by the relatively long, grass-like, linear leaves up to 80 mm long and usually terete distally. The fugaceous flowers are typical of ser. Occasionally the filaments are free in the upper third and the style may divide opposite the anthers rather than above them, possibly a developmental abberration. Moraea fugacissima is most easily confused with M. stagnalis but that species has broader leaves and smaller flowers with a perianth tube 5-10 mm long, a short style dividing opposite the anthers, and filaments typically free in the upper third.

description: Perennial herb, geophyte, 0.03-0.06 m high; solitary or forming thick clumps; corm with brown, fibrous tunics. Leaves 30-80 mm long, linear, grass-like, bifacial, canaliculate ± erect, spreading or falcate, unifacial distally, margins with hyaline borders, smooth or minutely ciliate. Inflorescence with pale yellow flowers in basal tufts; perianth tube 10-24 mm long; tepals 15-19 x 4-9 mm, subequal, ovate, obtuse. Stamens: filaments usually entirely united, 3-6 mm long; anthers 1.5-4.0 mm long, diverging. Ovary with style usually exceeding anthers; stigma fringed. Flowering time July-Sept. Acaulescent, cormous geophyte, 3-6 cm. Leaves linear to terete. Flowers yellow, tepals cupped, style exceeding anthers, stigmas fringed. Stemless, cormous geophyte, 30-60 mm tall. Leaves linear to terete, more-or-less erect. Flowers in a basal tuft, yellow, tubular below, tepals cupped, filaments united in a column, style exceeding anthers, style lobes fringed. Plant solitary or several in tufts, up to 70 mm high. Corm mostly 10-12 mm diam.; tunics fibrous, often with prominent vertical ribs. Stem underground at flowering. Leaves in a basal tuft, ± upright or lower ± prostrate, ± linear, narrowly channelled at least in lower half, often terete distally, 30-80 x ± 2 mm, margins of channelled part smooth or rarely sparsely minutely ciliate. Rhipidial spathes hardly distinct from leaves, with 2 to 5 flowers per plant. Flowers fugaceous, salver-shaped with tepals cupped below, uniformly yellow, sweetly scented; perianth tube cylindric, (10-)15-24 mm long; tepals subequal, obovate, (11-)15-19 x 4-9 mm. Filaments usually entirely united (free in upper 1/3), 3-6 mm long; anthers usually sessile, 1.5-4.0 mm long, yellow; pollen yellow. Ovary ± 2.5 mm long; style usually dividing ± 2 mm above anther tips, branches short, deeply fringed. Capsules and seeds unknown.

description: The rare M. galpinii is distinguished by the single, slender foliage leaf, usually barely emergent at flowering time but ultimately exceeding the stem. The blade appears at first to be terete but has a narrow adaxial groove separating the two closely appressed leaf halves. The flowers, fairly typical of subg. Grandiflorae, are bright yellow and have outer tepals 40-50 mm long with spreading limbs and erect inner tepals ± 35 mm long. Particularly distinctive is the collar of hard, blackish vertical fibres enclosing the base of the stem and extending a short distance above ground. This feature is shared with M. robusta, which is distinguished by paler, larger flowers with erect to spreading inner and outer tepal limbs. Young plants not yet of flowering age have rather soft, unbroken ± membranous cataphylls.

description: With one of the largest and most striking flowers in the genus, Moraea gigandra has dark blue-purple, or rarely white or orange flowers with broad, shortly clawed outer tepals up to 45 mm long and 30-35 mm wide, the limbs spreading horizontally and with dark blue to turquoise, crescent-shaped nectar guides. The flowers are distinctive not only in size but also for their extraordinarily long anthers, 13-15 mm long and exceeding the style branches. The style crests are barely developed and are about as long as the stigmatic lobes. The single, channelled leaf is usually hairy on the abaxial surface and the stems are velvety. Like other species in the M. villosa alliance the inner tepals are 3-lobed, with an elongate spreading to trailing central lobe. The species is comparatively late-flowering. Moraea gigandra was evidently once common north of the Berg River but is now on the verge of extinction.

description: Recognised by its solitary habit and relatively large flowers with the outer tepals 60-75 mm long. description: The most striking of the species of the Moraea tripetala complex, M. grandis has relatively large corms up to 15 mm diam., with tunics usually of fine, soft (rarely firm) fibres, and the largest flowers in the alliance. The outer tepals are 30-40 mm long with ± orbicular limbs 18-23 x 15-20 mm, thus almost as wide as long, and have unusually small nectar guides, usually yellow (sometimes ± white) on a white background, minutely spotted with dark blue, and usually edged with darker blue or violet. The limbs are also widest in the upper third and usually have an abrupt, comma-like tip. The flowers have a pleasant, vanilla-like odour. Like its relative, M. amabilis, it typically grows in colonies resulting from vegetative reproduction by axillary cormlets and sometimes by the replacement of the parent corm by two daughter corms. It also resembles M. amabilis in having virtually free filaments (united for < 0.2 mm), but the anthers, 8-11 mm long, are at least twice as long as the filaments and sometimes 2.5 times as long, easily the largest in the M. tripetala complex. The pollen is consistently bright orange-red, not unusual for the complex, but contrasting with the white pollen in most western Karoo populations of M. amabilis, which has smaller anthers 4.5-7.0 mm long and ± as long as or up to 1.5 times as long as the filaments. Moraea grandis sometimes grows in close proximity to M. amabilis, and the two can be seen flowering together at sites in the Calvinia District and occasionally elsewhere. Difficulty in distinguishing the two in the immediate vicinity of Nieuwoudtville is probably the result of hybridisation and introgression between the two species.

description: Stands out in its slender, terete leaf, often loosely spirally coiled, and in the small, violet flower with subequal tepals with spreading to reflexed limbs and short, almost vestigial style branches lacking crests. The flower is subsessile and the perianth is raised above the spathes on a sterile, tubular extension of the ovary, a structure that is paralleled in sect. Gynandriris. Moraea herrei is allied to two southern Namibian species, M. graniticola and M. rigidifolia, both of which have a shortly beaked ovary with the beak much shorter than in M. herrei. Moraea graniticola differs additionally in having a true perianth tube and a stem barely reaching above ground.

description: Plants 6-14 mm high. Corm up to 20 mm diam.; tunics of dark brown fibres, vertical members heavily thickened, accumulating in a dense mass, extending upward as a collar around base. description: With the smallest flowers in subg. Visciramosae, Moraea inconspicua is distinguished by its flowers with fully reflexed tepals, the outer mostly 12-18 mm long (rarely up to 25 mm), the limb at least twice as long as the claw. In addition the rhipidial spathes are short, usually less than 28 mm long and sometimes only 18 mm. Flower colour is variable, mostly yellow or partly to completely brown, but white-flowered morphs occur in the Biedouw Valley near Clanwilliam and on the Agulhas Plain near Elim, the latter with the smallest flowers recorded in the species. In Namaqualand flowers are sometimes ivory-coloured or pink, but also yellow or brown as elsewhere. The foliage leaves are usually straight and erect below but often trailing distally, and have channelled blades, but plants from Namaqualand have distinctive spirally coiled leaves with a plane surface and on this basis have been segregated as subsp. namaquensis. Populations from the northern Cederberg and Biedouw Valley have unusually large flowers for the species, the outer tepals up to 25 mm long, thus matching those of closely allied M. bituminosa. The narrow leaves, short style crests and almost fully reflexed tepal limbs conform to M. inconspicua. Superficially similar Moraea viscaria, is a white-flowered species with spreading tepals 15-23 mm long, a strong floral odour, and relatively well-developed style crests up to 6 mm long, half as long to ± as long as the style branches. Moraea saldanhensis may also be confused with M. inconspicua but has slate-blue flowers with the tepal claws as long as to slightly longer than the limbs, the latter usually reflexed to ± 45º.

description: Moraea kamiesmontana stands out in subg. Galaxia not only in its particularly small size but in the structure of its flowers. In other species of the subgenus the flowers have flaccid, widely cupped tepals that lack distinct claws, but in M. kamiesmontana the ascending tepal claws form a narrow cup enclosing the filaments and the limbs are sharply flexed at right angles to the cup, thus extended horizontally. The chromosome number, 2n = 18, is the ancestral number for the subgenus, and we interpret Moraea kamiesmontana as a relict species, surviving in specialised, seasonally moist, montane habitats.

description: Particularly tall for sect. Hexaglottis and standing up to 2 m high, Moraea longifolia is distinguished by the pale yellow flowers with faint nectar guides without dark spotting, comparatively short style branches, 4-6 mm long, and large, obovoid to club-shaped capsules. Moraea longifolia is tetraploid and known to be self-compatible and autogamous, whereas the other species of the section are diploid and self-incompatible (compatibility relations are not known for M. brevituba). Closely related and similar M. lewisiae has cylindric 3-lobed capsules, slightly larger, deeper yellow flowers with prominently spotted nectar guides, and style branches 6-7 mm long. Also sometimes confused with M. longifolia, M. riparia has smaller capsules and bright yellow, strongly scented flowers, and is self-incompatible.

description: Cormous geophyte, 60-150 cm. Leaves 3-5, linear, channelled and trailing. Flowers pale yellow. Capsules club-shaped, exserted from spathes, 12-20 mm. Perennial herb, geophyte, 0.6-1.5 m high; corm with tunics of fine light brown fibres; stem straight, simple or 1-3-branched. Leaves 3-5, linear, ascending, flat or canaliculate, bending or trailing above. Spathes cylindric, herbaceous, apex attenuate, dry. Inflorescence a spike; flowers pale yellow, stellate; tepals free, subequal, spreading, with claws ± 2 mm long. Stamens 4-6 mm long; filaments united for 2-3 mm; anthers 5-6 mm long. Ovary with long filiform beak, 8-12 mm long, exserted; style branches 4-6 mm long, ascending, reaching base of anthers. Flowering time Oct., Nov. Capsule obovoid-clavate, truncate. Plants 600-2000 mm high. Corm 15-20 mm diam.; tunics of fine, light brown fibres. Stem ± straight, simple or 1- to 3-branched from lower nodes, lateral rhipidia sessile, each subtended by sheathing leaf often entirely concealing rhipidia. Foliage leaves 3 or 4(5), linear, ascending below, bent and trailing distally, lowermost longest, 250-600 mm long, progressively shorter above, 6-12(-20) mm wide, ± flat or channelled. Rhipidial spathes attenuate, dry at tips, inner 3.5-5.5(-7.5) mm long, outer slightly shorter. Flowers fugaceous, stellate, pale yellow, usually only outer tepal limbs with inconspicuous, slightly darker yellow nectar guides, odourless or faintly scented; tepals with claws ± 2 mm long, clasping filament column, limbs spreading, outer with limbs 19-27 x 8-11 mm, inner 16-23 x 6-9 mm. Filaments 4-6 mm long, united in lower 2-3 mm; anthers 5-6 mm long before anthesis, yellow; pollen yellow. Ovary 8-12 mm long, exserted, style branches divided to base in filiform, horizontally extended arms 4-6 mm long. Capsules obovoid-clavate, truncate, 12-16(-23) mm long, exserted, splitting for 1/2 to 3/4 their length. Seeds angular, 2.0-2.3 mm long.

description: Flowering in mid-winter in May and June, Moraea longipes has the general aspect of M. ciliata and M. tricolor except that the stem is not subterranean at flowering but extends up to 180 mm above ground. Like most species of subg. Acaules the ovary is retracted to the base of the inflorescence spathes after flowering. The flowers are most like those of M. ciliata but have slightly broader style crests, triangular with the base 2.5-3.0 mm wide (± linear in M. ciliata) and the filaments are united basally for ± 1.5 mm, about one fifth of their length, as are those of most other species of subg. Acaules. The anthers of M. longipes are the longest in the subgenus, 7.5-9.0 mm long (5-8 mm in M. ciliata) and are held above the nectar guides on filaments as long as the tepal claws. A notable feature of M. longipes is the collar of fibres around the underground part of the stem, uncommon but not unique in the subgenus. The species flowers early in the season, May to early July, and grows in places where M. ciliata has been found in bloom six to eight weeks later. Flower colour in M. longipes is either pale, watery yellow or translucent white, then with the edges of the outer tepal limbs and the inner tepal limbs a pale coppery pink colour and with the tepals flushed the same colour outside.

description: Plants 100-180 mm high. Corm globose, 15-20 mm diam.; tunics of ± straw-coloured, coarse fibres often with thickened vertical ridges. Stem unbranched, consisting of a single internode extending from the corm to well above ground level, sheathed by fibrous collar around base. Foliage leaves 3 (including leaf-like outer spathe), subopposite, inserted at base of inflorescence, suberect, straight, 45-85 mm long, channelled, margins smooth or sparsely ciliate. Rhipidial spathe with broad, transparent membranous margins, 50-70 mm long. Flowers fugaceous. Pale yellow or translucent white with pale copper-pink margins of outer tepals, inner tepals and outside of tepals, outer tepal limbs with yellow nectar guides at bases speckled with black dots, laxly spreading; outer tepals ± 30 x 19 mm, claw suberect, ± 10 mm long, hairy in midline, inner tepals ± 28 x 2-4 mm, claws suberect, ± 9 mm long, limbs laxly spreading. Filaments suberect, 7-9 mm long, united basally for ± 1.5 mm; anthers 7.5-9.0 mm long, reaching base of stigma lobes. Ovary elongate, fertile part ovoid, 5-9 mm long, usually at least partly included; style branches ascending, 13-16 mm long, crests erect, narrowly triangular, outer margins slightly and unevenly serrated, 8-10 x 2.5-3.0 mm at base. Capsules and seeds unknown. Like M. ciliata but leaves borne on stems held well above ground, cataphylls forming a fibrous collar around base, flowers pale yellow or translucent white with tepal margins and reverse coppery red.

description: Immediately recognised by the small, violet to pale blue flower with feathery or fringed style crests, unique in Moraea and reminiscent of the related genus Ferraria. The species also recalls Ferraria in the stigmatic surfaces located at the lateral tips of style branches. Both floral morphology and molecular phylogenetic studies place M. lugubris close to the base of phylogenetic trees, in some it is retrieved as sister to the remaining species of Moraea. The corm is of the Moraea type, thus consisting of a single internode with an apical bud and enclosed by well-developed tunics. The tunics of coarse fibres loosely enclosing the corm body are, however, unique in the genus.

description: Cormous geophyte, 6-16 cm. Leaves 2 or 3, linear, channelled. Flowers deep blue, style branches feathery. Plants 60-160 mm high. Flowers fugaceous, blue to violet, outer tepal limbs with yellow nectar guides at bases; outer tepals 16-18 mm long, claws ± 5 mm long, reflexed to ± 45º; inner tepals ± as long but narrower, similarly reflexed. Ovary narrowly ovoid, 2-3 mm long, usually exserted; style branches plane, bearing stigmatic areas at lateral tips, with single prominent crest and feathery outgrowths from distal surface. Capsules ± globose, 6-8 mm long. Seeds angular prismatic.

description: Acaulescent, cormous geophyte, 2-5 cm. Leaves ovate and prostrate, conspicuously ciliate. Flowers yellow fading to white at edges, tepals cupped, stamens free, style exceeding anthers, stigmas fringed. Plants up to 50 mm high, often growing in small clumps. Corm 12-16 mm diam.; tunics of fine fibres accumulating in a dense mass. Stem underground at flowering. Foliage leaves not clearly distinguished from rhipidial spathes, inserted at ground level, ovate, lower 2 prostrate, ovate-oblong, ± plane, 20-40 x up to 6 mm, margins hyaline, densely ciliate. Rhipidial spathes not distinct from leaves; with 2 to 5 flowers per plant. Flowers fugaceous, ± salver-shaped, usually deep yellow in centre with tepals grading to creamy white distally or uniformly yellow; perianth tube cylindric, 7-16 mm long; tepals obovate, ± obtuse, 15-21 x 7-10 mm. Filaments 5.5-7.5 mm long, united in lower ± 2 mm, diverging above; anthers 2-3 mm long, yellow; pollen yellow. Ovary ovoid, ± 3 mm long; style slender, initially erect, dividing above anther tips, later eccentric, stigma lobes fringed. Capsules and seeds unknown.

description: Allied to the well-known and widespread Moraea ciliata and occurring entirely within the range of this species, M. macronyx can be distinguished by its larger flowers with the outer tepal claws one and a half to twice as long as the limbs. The larger outer tepals are 40-60 mm long with the claws 25-40 mm long and the style branches are ± 20 mm long with crests up to 25 mm long. The outer tepals of M. ciliata are mostly 25-35 mm long with the claws 12-15 mm long, thus about half as long as the limbs, and the style branches are typically 8-15 mm long. Vegetatively M. macronyx and M. ciliata are nearly identical although the corm tunics may differ, those of M. macronyx sometimes unusual in being entire and peculiarly soft, of an almost spongy, pith-like texture. Some populations, however, have fibrous corm tunics no different from those of M. ciliata.

description: Moraea margaretae has the brown, ± woody corm tunics, leathery rhipidial spathes with brown tips and flowers with finely brown-veined yellow tepals characteristic of subg. Umbellatae, and is distinguished in the subgenus by its habit and flowers with well-developed style branches and prominent style crests. The leaves and branches (when present) are crowded close to ground level and the aerial stem and branches comprise a single internode. The species is tetraploid, 2n = 40 (two populations counted), one of the few exclusively polyploid species known in Moraea. Moraea margaretae seems to be most closely related to M. orthrosantha of central Namaqualand but this species has aerial stems of three or four internodes, with two or three branches at the aerial nodes. The flowers of the two are similar in size and colour but those of M. margaretae have shorter filaments ± 5 mm long vs. filaments 8-9 mm long in M. orthrosantha. Both species have red anthers and pollen. Hybrids between M. margaretae and M. intermedia occur at a site west of Springbok.

description: Distinguished in subg. Grandiflorae by its solitary habit, long, narrow, channelled leaf 11-15 mm wide, often with a grey blush, and very large, pale yellow to white flowers. The outer tepals are up to 75 mm long and the inner up to 60 mm long. It is most easily confused with M. spathulata, some forms of which are similar, but the two can usually be distinguished by the solitary habit of M. moggii compared with typically clump-forming M. spathulata, which has broader leaves often flat or very widely channelled and usually darker yellow flowers. Apart from this, M. moggii is generally a late flowering species, while M. spathulata flowers in spring or summer, except for some southern KwaZulu-Natal populations that also flower late in the season. Two subspecies are recognised, northern subsp. moggii, with pale yellow flowers, and southern subsp. albescens which typically has white or creamy yellow flowers.

description: Cormous geophyte, 10-20 cm, branching only from base. Leaves 3 or 4, often pilose. Flowers yellow or salmon. Plants 60-160 mm high. Corm 8-13 mm diam.; tunics of flat, brown, woody sections separated by cross fibres, ultimately decaying into fibrous mass. Stem roughly hairy to ± smooth, usually (1)2 internodes long above insertion of basal foliage leaf or leaves, several-branched from base or from upper node (rarely unbranched), basal internode elongating in fruit. Foliage leaves 2 to 4, linear to falcate but spreading distally, sometimes loosely twisted, lowermost ± basal or inserted at first above ground node, channelled below, ± as long or longer than stem, finely to roughly hairy on veins, rarely smooth, occasionally veins prominently thickened, intervein areas ± smooth or papillate, margins undulate, long-ciliate. Rhipidial spathes often with dry brown apices or entirely green, acute, usually hairy on veins and margins, inner 24-30 (subsp. Glabrescens) or (35-)40-60 (subsp. Papilionacea) mm long, outer usually slightly shorter than inner, rarely ± 1/2 as long, sometimes not sheathing distally. description: One of the tallest species of subg. description: Recognised by the branched stem bearing two to four foliage leaves, and moderate-sized, blue to blue-mauve, violet or rarely white flowers with style branches as narrow and as long as or slightly longer than the anthers and lacking style crests. The filaments are united in a slender, smooth column usually 7-9 mm long. A notable variant of the species from near Albertinia and Herbertsdale in southern Western Cape has slightly smaller, white or pale blue flowers with the filaments only 5-6 mm long, and both filaments and anthers are included in the floral cup whereas the anthers are usually fully excluded from the cup in typical M. polyanthos. The species is closely allied to M. bipartita, which has conventional Moraea-type flowers with broad style branches with prominent crests but the two are identical in vegetative features. description: One of the taller species in the genus, plants often exceeding 1 m in height, and exhibits such ancestral features as multiple foliage leaves and an unspecialised yellow flower. Notably the filaments are free or barely united at the base, evidently a derived condition. Peculiar to the species are the hard, spiny roots that enclose the corm and hundreds of cormlets produced around the base. The spiny roots probably have a protective function but they evidently do not prevent massive depredation by baboons and porcupines that uproot large numbers of plants in search of the edible corms. The survival of such populations is assured by the production of cormlets which are shed in large numbers from the base of the main corm and also from the lower aerial nodes. The corm tunics, often decayed at flowering, consist of firm, leathery, brown layers that split from the base.

description: Late-flowering Moraea saxicola is recognised by the solitary foliage leaf with thickened, straight to undulate margins, and relatively large flowers with outer tepals 34-45 mm long and the limbs of both whorls half reflexed. The tepals are usually pale blue in the north of its range, white to palest yellow elsewhere, and the outer tepal limbs bear pale yellow nectar guides. The foliage leaf is fairly broad and slightly undulate with occasionally slightly crisped margins. Unusual for Moraea, the juvenile leaves are narrow and sometimes terete and coiled near the apex. By the time these plants reach flowering age, the leaf is usually broad, channelled and trailing. Moraea saxicola is allied to the yellow-flowered M. bolusii of northern Namaqualand, which also has an undulate leaf.

description: Cormous geophyte, 120-800 mm tall. Leaf 1, linear, channelled, often trailing, margins often undulate, occasionally crisped (juvenile leaves terete and coiled distally). Flowers enclosed in partly dry spathes, white to pale blue-mauve, tepal limbs lightly reflexed, the inner slightly smaller, style branches broad, crests prominent. Mostly Sept. Plants mostly 200-500 mm high. Corms 16-20 mm diam.; tunics dark brown, finely netted, extending upward in a thick collar around base. Stem (4)5 to 8 internodes long, branched, sometimes with 1 or 2 longer branches from lower nodes, upper nodes bearing ± sessile rhipidia or branches short and concealed by attenuate sheathing leaves, mostly 35-45 mm long. Foliage leaf solitary, usually exceeding stem, channelled to ± flat, 4-9 mm wide, falcate or trailing distally, sometimes twisted or loosely coiled distally, margins pale, thickened, straight or undulate, occasionally partly crisped, (juvenile leaves straight or somewhat twisted, narrowly channelled, up to 2 mm wide, or terete). Rhipidial spathes becoming dry at flowering time, often lacerated, inner 40-60 mm long, outer ± 10 mm shorter. Flowers fugaceous, pale blue or white to pale watery yellow, outer tepal limbs with long yellow to orange nectar guides white in middle at bases, faintly scented; outer tepals 34-45 mm long, limbs mostly 15-22 x 10-16 mm, half reflexed, claws ± as long or slightly shorter than limbs; inner tepals 30-36 mm long, limbs reflexed. Filaments 12-14 mm long, united in lower half; anthers 6-9 mm long, slightly exceeding stigma lobe, pale mauve; pollen white. Ovary ± cylindric, 8-10 mm long; included, style branches 8-15 mm long, crests ± lanceolate, 12-18 mm long. Capsules ellipsoid, mostly 12-14 mm long, with short beak up to 1 mm long. Seeds angular.

description: Somewhat variable across its wide range, Moraea spathulata typically forms large tufts, thus it is not unusual to see several flowers open at once. Each flowering stem bears a single broad leaf, shallowly channelled to almost flat. The species can be distinguished by its large yellow flowers, the outer tepals up to 50 mm long, tall stems, and clump-forming habit. Plants flower in late winter and spring along the coast but in summer and autumn inland. The species comprises numerous local races, but owing to the small differences between them, it is difficult to define many of them. Four subspecies were described in Goldblatt (1973) but are not currently recognised.

description: Capsules 3.5–5.5 cm long, oblong-cylindric. Plants large, 80–120 cm high, usually in small clumps or occasionally solitary. description: Cormous geophyte to 1 m, unbranched. Leaf solitary, linear, flat or channelled, often fairly broad. Flowers large, yellow, inner tepals erect. Cormous herb, up to 0.9 m high. Plants usually in clumps. Leaf flat above, 15 mm wide. Cataphylls usually dark brown and often unbroken. Flowers yellow with deep yellow nectar guides. Plants up to 1 m high, usually in clumps, rarely solitary, evergreen. Corm 15-20 mm diam.; tunics brown, fibrous, often accumulating in a loose mass. Stem sheathed below by brown, sometimes netted cataphylls, simple, rarely with a sessile lateral rhipidium from penultimate node, sheathed entirely by pale green, ± inflated, sheathing leaves 90-180 mm long, tips usually dry and brown. Foliage leaf solitary, much longer than stem, linear, flat to shallowly channelled, 18-24 wide. Rhipidial spathes acute to attenuate, inner 100-180 mm long, outer slightly shorter. Flowers long-lasting, yellow often with dark veins, outer tepal limbs with deeper yellow to orange nectar guides at bases, reflexed to ± 45º, faintly honey-scented; outer tepals 35-50 x 20-25 mm, claws ± 1/3 as long as limbs; inner tepals 30-60 mm long, suberect or curving inward distally. Filaments 8-16 mm long, united in lower half; anthers 7-15 mm long, purple or white. Ovary cylindric, 20-30 mm long, cylindric-triangular; style branches 20-30 mm long, crests erect, up to 20 mm long. Capsules oblong-cylindric, broadly 3-lobed, mostly 30-45 mm long. Seeds flattened, discoid, ± 3 mm diam. Perennial herb, geophyte, 0.35-1.50 m high, solitary or in clumps; corm tunics of brown, coarse fibres; stem simple, sheathed with large overlapping bracts. Leaf 1, linear, flat or canaliculate, trailing above. Spathes herbaceous, apex dry, attenuate. Inflorescence with yellow flowers; nectar guides dark yellow; tepals unequal, outer 35-50 mm long, reflexed, inner 30-40 mm long, entire, with expanded limb, erect. Stamens: filaments 8-12 mm long, united in lower half; anthers 8-12 mm long. Ovary 20-30 mm long; style branches 12-18 mm long; crests up to 10 mm long. Flowering time Apr.-Dec. Capsule cylindric. Cormous geophyte, up to 0.9 m high; cataphylls usually dark brown and often unbroken. Leaf solitary, flat above, 15 mm wide, twisted. Flowers: perianth with outer segments 35-50 mm long, yellow with deep yellow nectar guides on outer segments; Nov.-Feb.

description: The wet habitat is distinctive for Moraea stagnalis, which has flowers almost identical with those of other members of ser. Galaxia but with the filaments usually free in the upper third. The style divides opposite the anthers and the stigmatic fringes of the style branches are always in contact with the anthers and pollen. The narrow, shallowly channelled leaves have smooth to minutely ciliate margins. Moraea stagnalis is polyploid, 2n = 36, and in the laboratory is autogamous. The species is most easily confused with M. fugacissima, which has larger flowers with a perianth tube mostly 15-24 mm long, anthers up to 4 mm long, and the style usually exceeding the anthers rather than tangled among them. The filaments of M. fugacissima are usually completely united whereas those of M. stagnalis are typically, though not invariably, free in the upper third.

description: Readily distinguished in sect. Vieusseuxia by the comparatively large, white or sometimes pale creamy yellow flowers with spreading, comparatively broad tepal limbs forming a wide cup. The inner tepal limbs are 3-lobed with rounded lateral lobes and a slender central lobe up to 5 mm long, usually obliquely coiled inward (sometimes straight in subsp. parviflora). Closely allied to M. bellendenii and sometimes barely distinguishable from it without knowledge of flower colour, M. tricuspidata is a shorter plant, rarely exceeding 500 mm in height, whereas M. bellendenii has deep yellow flowers and is a taller, more slender species, 500-1000 mm high. Slight but apparently consistent differences in size of floral parts can usually be relied upon to distinguish them. Although they have somewhat different habitat preferences and flowering times, the two occasionally grow close to one another at sites on the Cape Peninsula, where hybrids between the two occur, these intermediate in height and with pale yellow flowers.

description: With a reddish purple flower with yellow cup, Moraea variabilis most resembles M. versicolor but differs in the glossy, dark green leaves, channelled with straight margins, filaments usually united entirely or rarely free for less than 1 mm, thus with the anthers sessile or almost so, and the style dividing just above the anther tips. description: Acaulescent, cormous geophyte, 2-5 cm. Leaves ovate to oblong, channelled, prostrate. Flowers purple to mauve with yellow centre, tepals cupped, anthers sessile, style exceeding anthers, stigmas lobed. Plants acaulescent, up to 40 mm high. Corm ± globose, 10-15 mm diam.; tunics of dark brown, netted fibres arranged in herringbone pattern, vertical ribs often thick and woody, often accumulating in a dense mass. Stem underground at flowering. Leaves in a basal tuft, ± straight, spreading, lowermost often ± prostrate, oblong to lanceolate, channelled to flat, 30-50 x ± 6 mm, margins ± straight, minutely ciliate. Rhipidial spathes hardly distinct from leaves, with up to 5 flowers per plant. Flowers fugaceous, salver-shaped with tepals cupped in lower halves, usually dark pink-purple with yellow cup and darkly pigmented at edge of cup; perianth tube cylindric, 12-30 mm long; tepals subequal, spreading distally, obovate, 20-35 x 10-13 mm. Filaments ± 6 mm long, united in smooth, straight column, rarely free in distal ± 1 mm, usually yellow; anthers sessile (or nearly so), ± erect, 3-4 mm long before splitting, yellow or purple; pollen yellow. Ovary oblong-cylindric, ± 4 mm long; style straight, dividing above anther tips into 3 short, spreading stigmatic lobes, margins undulate. Capsules and seeds unknown.

description: Moraea venenata has the several leaves, a branched stem, and blue-violet flowers much like those of M. polystachya, but is a more robust species, although often not as tall. The flowers have outer tepals 40-60 mm long with the claws 22-30 mm long, and as far as known the inner tepals are erect. The widest of the several leaves are up to 30 mm wide near the middle [vs. 6-12(-20) mm in M. polystachya] and the outer spathes are up to 60 mm long and the inner about half as long but with unusually broad, translucent margins, free almost to the base, an unusual feature among the southern African members of the genus.

description: Plants medium to large, 200-300 mm high. Corm globose, 20-35 mm diam.; tunics of hard, dark medium-textured to coarse fibres. Stem several-branched, with green to partly to completely dry, attenuate sheathing leaves at upper nodes 30-50 mm long. Foliage leaves 3 to 6, lanceolate to linear, channelled to ± flat, as long or longer than stem, falcate, usually trailing distally, 8-30 mm wide, margins often thickened, hyaline. Rhipidial spathes green or turning brown and dry above, long attenuate, with broad, translucent margins, inner mostly 40-60 mm long, outer almost as long, margins free nearly to base. Flowers fugaceous, blue-violet, outer tepal limbs with yellow to orange nectar guides at bases, reflexed up to ± 40º; outer tepals mostly 45-60 x 18-25 mm, claws ± 22 mm long, inner 35-50 x 9-12 mm, evidently ± erect. Filaments 10-15 mm long, united in lower 2/3; anthers 8-9 mm long. Ovary ± cylindric, mostly 15-20 mm long, sometimes veined red, usually included; style branches ± 12 mm long, crests up to 15 mm long. Capsules narrowly obovoid, 16-20 mm long, nodding when mature. Seeds angular, ± 2 mm long.

description: Plants 30-45 cm. high. Filaments 1.2-1.5 cm. long, united in the lower 1/2-2/3; anthers 8-10(-11) mm. long. Foliage leaf solitary, exceeding the stem, linear, channelled, 3-7 mm. wide. Cataphylls pale to dark brown, broken and becoming fibrous. Stem unbranched, with 3-6 sheathing leaves, these imbricate, 5-8 cm. long, overlapping the base of the rhipidial spathes. Rhipidial spathes often entirely green or dry apically, the inner 8-12 cm. long, outer 1/2-2/3 as long as the inner. Flowers pale yellow to whitish, the outer tepals with pale yellow nectar guides toward the bases of the limbs (blue with white nectar guides in Zairean and some Zambian populations). Outer tepals lanceolate, 4-5.5 cm. long, the limb usually slightly shorter than the claw, and reflexed; inner tepals erect, strongly spathulate, 3.7-4.4 cm. long.

description: Moraea versicolor has pink to purple flowers with tepals forming a cup in the lower half, usually with a yellow centre but populations with a blue to violet centre occur locally. The leaves are usually somewhat glaucous and widely channelled and often somewhat twisted, with undulate margins. The filaments are free and diverging in the upper 1.0-1.5 mm and united in the lower part, usually forming a bottle-shaped column wider in the lower half but populations with a cylindric filament column occur in the Breede River Valley. The style divides above the anthers, often exceeding them by 3-4 mm. Moraea variabilis has similarly coloured flowers but glossy, channelled leaves with straight margins, and filaments united entirely or rarely free distally for less than 1 mm, with the style dividing just above the anther tips. The species is variable for chromosome number and most populations have a diploid number of 2n = 16 but plants from the northern Cape Peninsula and from the Tulbagh Valley have 2n = 14.

description: Closely resembling the common and widespread Moraea gawleri in all vegetative features, notably the strongly vertically ribbed corm tunics, and short rhipidial spathes with the outer much shorter than the inner, M. vlokii usually has a single foliage leaf (occasionally a second much shorter one), always with straight margins, and pale yellow flowers with short tepal claws less than one quarter as long as the limbs, and vestigial style branches shorter than and concealed by the anthers and lacking crests. By contrast, M. gawleri has tepal claws only slightly shorter than the limbs and style branches with prominent, petaloid crests. Both species have broadly obovoid to almost globose capsules. Flowers open in early morning and collapse at ± 13:00, whereas those of M. gawleri open in mid- to late morning and last through late afternoon.

description: Cormous geophyte, 15-20 cm. Leaves 1 or 2, linear, channelled. Flowers tiny, yellow, style branches reduced, concealed by anthers, crests vestigial. Plants 140-330 mm high. Foliage leaves 1(2), lower ± basal, upper when present inserted from lowest aerial node, linear, channelled, usually slightly longer than stem, mostly 1.5-2.5 mm wide, margins straight. Rhipidial spathes green, becoming dry and brown apically, ± acute, inner ± 10 mm long, outer slightly shorter. Flowers fugaceous, yellow, limbs of all tepals with yellow nectar guides at bases, ± spreading to reflexed to 30º, unscented; claws ascending, ± 2.5 mm long, forming a cup enclosing lower half of filaments; outer tepals ± 14 x 9 mm, inner tepals ± 10 x 7 mm. Filaments ± 7 mm long, united in a smooth column, diverging in upper 1 mm; anthers ± 2 mm long, yellow; pollen yellow. Ovary narrowly obovoid, ± 2 mm long, style branches ± 2 mm long, appressed to and reaching upper 1/3 of anther, forked apically, without crests. Capsules ± globose to broadly ovoid, ± 4 mm long. Seeds angled.

description: With the spreading, ± fringed stigmatic lobes of ser. Galaxia, Moraea vuvuzela stands out in its pale yellow flowers with brown or purplish markings at the top of the darker yellow floral cup. Most of the remaining members of the series have uniformly bright yellow flowers. The corm tunics of M. vuvuzela are ± woody with prominent, thickened longitudinal ribs only partially separated from one another by transverse fibres. The corm tunics in most other species are less woody, with the longitudinal ribs separated by transverse fibres, with the exception of M. angulata, which has unique, woody or corky tunics with wing-like longitudinal ribs.

Corolla cream to yellow, the tube mostly greenish and the lobes bright yellow inside; tube 1.6–2.4 cm. long, widened at the apex, puberulous; lobes 3–7 x 1.2–4 mm., ovate-lanceolate, margined and with thickened apices, hairy inside particularly near throat with yellow hairs; throat densely hairy. description: Sepals rose, linear-oblong, 0.9-1.2 cm. long, 3-4 mm. wide, deflexed, pubescent at the apex; petals paler rose to bright pink, often white at base or yellowish, linear, 1.2-1.5 cm. long, 3 mm. wide. Flowers in sparsely pilose inflorescences appearing when the plant is leafless; rachis 4 cm. long; bracts oblong, 1.5 mm. long, 1 mm. wide, obtuse, sparsely pilose; stalks elongate, cylindrical, articulate, 0.5-2 cm. long, true pedicels short. Receptacle tubular, 1.3-3 cm. long, 2 mm. wide. Leaves (1(cult.) -)2-3-pinnate, 15-40 cm. long, with 2 pairs of pinnae and with 3-5 leaflets, densely pubescent when very young, later glabrescent; leaflets oblong, elliptic or obovate, 2.5-6(-7 cult.) cm. long, 1.5-4.5(-5.2 cult.) cm. wide, rounded or emarginate but apiculate at the apex, cuneate, rounded or subcordate at the base, glabrous or finely puberulous, the venation ± prominent beneath; petioles up to 2.5 cm. long. Ovary 5 mm. long, 1.5 mm. wide, glabrous, the stipe 5 mm. long; style white, filiform, up to 2 cm. long in young fruit but mostly as long as staminodes. Shrub or subshrub, often with a single slender brittle stem or several virgate stems 0.9-3 m. tall, but some flowering shoots may be as little as 10 cm. long, grey pilose when young but soon glabrous; bark purple-brown or dark grey, finely longitudinally ridged when dry; tuber up to the size of a rugby football, about 30 cm. below ground. Stamens attached to margin of receptacle on very narrow annulus, filaments 1.2 cm. long; anthers yellow-green, 2 mm. long, 1.5 mm. wide; staminodes 5, episepalous, ± as long as stamen-filaments. Seeds yellow-green or colourless, the body 1-1.3 cm. long, 8-9 mm. wide, transversely ridged and pitted, the wings 2-3 cm. long overall, separated by wide sinuses at the extremities. Pods purple-brown with bloom or purple-striped, 13.5-30 cm. long, 1.2-1.4(-2.1) cm. wide, each valve with 2 grooves. Fig. 2/5, 6, 10.

description: Erect glabrous shrub or small tree, 1–5 m. tall, sparsely divaricately branched; young branches lenticellate; bark greyish, somewhat scaly and eventually longitudinally fissured. Fruit almost square in outline, 2.3 cm. across, 1.2 cm. thick; calyx-limb persistent; pyrene ellipsoid, ± 2–3 cm. long, 1.2–2 cm. wide, 1.1 cm. thick, the walls thickly woody with longitudinal ridges. Flowers (4–)5-merous, borne in pedunculate 15–35-flowered cymes arising at nodes from which the leaves have been shed; peduncle 1–1.5 cm. long, glabrous or sparsely pubescent on either side; pedicels 2–4 mm. long, pubescent on either side; bracteoles linear or subulate, up to 2 mm. long. Leaves restricted to new growth at apices of branches; blades oblong to broadly elliptic, 5.5–10 cm. long, 3–5 cm. wide, shortly acuminate or sometimes obtuse at apex, acute at base (? or rounded), stiffly papery, chestnut to blackish brown above, glaucous to pale brown beneath when dry; lateral nerves in 5–6 main pairs; tertiary nerves coarsely reticulate and sometimes rather difficult to observe beneath; domatia present as tufts of hair; petiole 0.6–1 cm. long; stipules sheath-like, 1–3 mm. long, bearing a caducous linear somewhat keeled lobe 3–5 mm. long. Corolla green, rather thick, wrinkled when dry, blunt in bud; tube 2–3 mm. long, villous at the throat, then with a ring of deflexed hairs 1/3 to halfway from the top; lobes oblong or triangular, ± 4 mm. long, thickened and subobtuse at apex. Stigmatic knob shortly exserted, slightly longer than wide, 1.5 mm. long, bifid at apex. Calyx usually coriaceous, drying yellow-green or sometimes greyish; tube ±1.5 mm. long; limb distinctly wider than tube, 2–3 mm. long, lobed to ± the middle; lobes oblong or lanceolate to ovate, obtuse to rounded, eventually spreading.

description: Shrub or dwarf shrub, up to 0.15 m high. Leaves fascicled; blade linear, oblong or narrowly obovate, primary leaf 4-7 mm long, apex shortly apiculate. Flowers: axillary, pedicels very short; sepals quite glabrous or inner minutely ciliate; side petals ± as long as carina; corolla 4.0-5.5 mm long, pink or white; Dec.-Apr. Fruit sparsely hispid, horns ± as long as capsule. Seeds broadly ellipsoid, caruncle with broad membranous lobes. A branched shrub or undershrub, from 10-150 cm high, erect or spreading. Young branches puberulous, becoming glabrous. Leaves fasciculate, the fascicles usually distinct, rarely crowded and concealing the stem, the vegetative and floral leaves not very different: the primary 4-0-7-0 mm long, almost flat at first, becoming fleshy later, linear, oblong or oblanceolate, shortly apiculate, glabrous or minutely puberulous: the secondary similar but occasionally some broader. Bracts 0-4- 0-8 mm long, ovate, concave, obtuse, glabrous. Flowers 4-0-5-5 mm long, pink or white, very shortly pedicellate. Sepals quite glabrous or the inner minutely ciliate, the anterior pair rather smaller than the others; the outer ovate, concave, obtuse or sub-acute: the inner almost flat, elliptical, from one-third to a little less than half the length of the side petals. Side petals widest a little below the middle, tapering to an acute or sub-acute tip, about as long as the carina. Claw of the carina usually shorter than the oblong limb, the line of attachment of the crest rather short, the width of the crest as great as or less than the limb of the carina, the upper and lower lobes similar. Ovary hispid in the upper part, horned, the anterior branch of the style small, the posterior well developed, making an obtuse angle with the style, the stigma somewhat oblique. Capsule sparsely hispid, the slender horns about as long as the capsule. Seed broadly ellipsoidal, sparsely pubescent, the caruncle with broad membranous lobes. Perennial shrub or dwarf shrub, young branches puberulous, becoming glabrous, 0.1-1.5 m high. Leaves fasciculate, fascicles usually distinct, rarely crowded and concealing stem. Bracts ovate, concave, obtuse, glabrous. Flowers pink or white, very shortly pedicellate. Sepals quite glabrous, outer pair ovate, concave, inner pair flat, elliptical. Side petals widest below middle, ± as long as carina. Flowering time Oct.-Jan. Fruit a sparsely hispid capsule, slender horns ± as long as capsule. Seed broadly ellipsoidal, sparsely pubescent.

description: A branched shrub, 30-60 cm high. Stems hispid or pubescent. Leaves fasciculate, pungent: the primary 8.0-10.0 mm long, acicular, channelled, patent, sometimes recurved, shortly hispid along the margin and on the prominent midrib below: the secondary similar but smaller, straight. Bracts 1.0-1.5 mm long, broadly oblong, concave, obtuse, sometimes shortly mucronate, the midrib evident, ciliolate. Flowers 4.5-5.5 mm long, pale pink, sessile. Sepals elliptical apiculate acute minutely ciliate: the outer concave: the inner almost flat, slightly longer than the outer, a little shorter than the side petals. Side petals linear widened slightly near the middle, obtuse, about as long as the carina. Claw of the carina about as long as the limb, the limb with a conspicuous swelling on either side: the line of attachment of the crest oblique, the width of the crest slightly less than the length of the carina, the upper lobes larger than the lower. Ovary with well-developed acute horns: the style stout, the anterior branch obtuse, small, the posterior very short, the stigma almost sessile. Capsule rather broad, with acute somewhat leaf-like horns, minutely scabrous along the margin, glabrous elsewhere, the horns as long as or slightly shorter than the capsule. Seed ellipsoidal, hispid, the hairs caducous, the caruncle with small membranous lobes on the adaxial side.

description: An erect shrub, 40 cm high or less, with slender branches. Young stems sparsely covered with very short curled hairs. Leaves fasciculate, straight, somewhat crowded, spine-tipped: the primary 6.0-9.0 mm long, linear-subulate, flat above, somewhat keeled below, glabrous, sparsely and shortly ciliate: the secondary variable in length, narrowing at the base but otherwise similar to the primary. Bracts 0.6-0.8 mm long, orbicular or ovate, concave, obtuse, sometimes mucronate, glabrous. Flowers 7-0-8-0 mm long, pink, very shortly pedicellate. Sepals glabrous, acuminate: the outer ovate, concave: the inner elliptical, almost flat, rather less than half the length of the side petals. Side petals linear-lanceolate, tapering to an acute apex, longer than the carina. Claw of the carina a little shorter than the limb: the line of attachment of the crest short, almost vertical; the width of the crest somewhat less than the length of the carina, the upper and lower lobes similar. Ovary almost glabrous, with slender erect horns: the style slender, the anterior branch small, the posterior long, more or less at right angles to the style, the stigma oblique. Capsule sparsely hispid above, the slender horns as long as or a little longer than the capsule. Seed ellipsoidal, hispid, the caruncle with short membranous lobes. Perennial, spreading, much-branched shrub, 0.15-1.20 m high. Leaves sessile, fascicled, somewhat crowded, narrowly elliptic, hooked above and spine-tipped. Flowers axillary, sessile, white, sometimes pink. Sepals glabrous, acuminate, outer pair ovate, concave, inner pair elliptical, flat, < 1/2 length of side petals. Side petals linear-lanceolate, longer than carina. Flowering time July-Dec. Fruit a capsule, slender horns slightly longer than capsule.

description: Spreading, much-branched shrub, up to 0.6 m tall, with puberulous young stems. Leaves clustered or solitary, linear or linear-lanceolate, 7-12 mm long, spine-tipped and hooked, margin scabrous, secondary ones smaller. Flowers sessile, white or pale pink, sepals two thirds as long as side petals. Capsule sparsely to minutely hispid, with prominent horns. A spreading much branched shrub up to 60 cm high. Young stems puberulous, becoming rather rough later. Leaves fasciculate or solitary the internodes usually conspicuous: the primary 7.0-12.0 mm long, linear or linear-lanceolate, acute, spine-tipped, uncinate, flat or occasionally slightly channelled near the apex, more or less glabrous, the margin scabrous, the midrib prominent below: the secondary similar but smaller. Bracts 1.4-1.6 mm long, oblong or broadly ovate, concave, obtuse, ciliolate. Flowers 5.0-7.0 mm long, white or pale pink, sessile. Sepals elliptical, obtuse or sub-acute, minutely apiculate, ciliate, the midrib prominent, the lateral veins visible: the outer concave: the inner larger, almost flat, about two-thirds as long as the side petals. Side petals linear, very slightly widened near the middle, obtuse, shorter than the carina. Claw of the carina about as long as the limb, the limb with a spongy swelling on either side: the line of attachment of the crest oblique, the width of the crest slightly greater than the length of the carina, the upper lobes larger than the lower. Ovary hispid above, the horns tapering: the anterior style branch small, the posterior rather long, the stigma oblique. Capsule broad, sparsely and minutely hispid, the tapering flat horns longer than the capsule. Seed oblong, softly and sparsely hairy, the caruncle with well-developed and oblique membranous lobes on the adaxial side.

description: A shrub or small tree 3–9(–?27) m. tall; young branches covered with dense to sparse, short adpressed hairs or rarely red spreading hairs, becoming glabrous with age, lenticels conspicuous, numerous, whitish and slightly prominent. Leaf-blades elliptic, 7–21 cm. long, 2.9–11 cm. wide, apex acuminate, base cuneate, with 6–13 pairs of lateral nerves, glabrescent to sparsely hairy on both surfaces with dense hairs, occasionally much longer red hairs on the nerves beneath; petioles 0.4–2.3 cm. long; stipules narrowly triangular, 3–13 mm. long, with adpressed hairs outside, caducous. Distance from the throat to the top of the anthers 5–10 mm. in long-styled flowers and 0–4 mm. in short-styled flowers. Style 1.9–2.8 cm. in long-styled flowers and 0–4 mm. in short-styled flowers; arms absent; stigma included, lobes 4–7 mm. long. Fruit green, dotted with brown lenticels, globose, sometimes slightly bilobed, 6–10 mm. long, with annular whitish buff scar encircling the blackish remains of the disc, sparsely covered with short hairs. Seeds golden-brown to blackish, ± oblong to square in outline, 0.6–0.8 mm. long, thickened and angular, distinctly reticulate. Corolla with tube greenish yellow and lobes lemon-yellow above; tube 2.8–4 cm. long, 3–6 mm. wide at top, 1.5–3 mm. wide at base, densely covered with buff or pink adpressed hairs outside, flattened hairs absent but with fine hairs present at the throat and extending between the anthers, becoming sparse for the remainder of the tube; lobes ovate, 5–12 mm. long, 3–7 mm. wide, acuminate at the apex with acumen 1–4 mm. long, the inner portion free or connate for up to 0.4 mm. long, with adpressed hairs below and short sparse hairs and longer yellow hairs on the midrib above. Calyx covered with adpressed hairs; tube green, turbinate, 2.5–5 mm. long; lobes brown, subulate to narrowly triangular or linear, 2.5–12 mm. long, up to 1 mm. wide, caducous; foliaceous lobes white to cream, ovate to broadly ovate, 3.2–9.3 cm. long, 2.5–8.2 cm. wide, acute to acuminate at apex, truncate at base, glabrescent or covered with velvety hairs; stipe 1–2.1 cm. long. Flowers heterostylous or isostylous, sweet-scented, in ± dense panicles; peduncles 1.2–4.7 cm. long; secondary peduncles present; pedicels 3–5.5 mm. long; 0–8 foliaceous calyx-lobes present on each inflorescence; bracts and bracteoles inconspicuous, 1–3-lobed, up to 7 mm. long, caducous or persistent.

description: Shrub or small tree, sometimes scandent, 2.4–9.6 m. tall; branches covered with spreading hairs or more rarely with very sparse adpressed hairs; lenticels whitish, small, inconspicuous. Leaf-blades elliptic to ovate, 9.8–18 cm. long, 4.5–10.9 cm. wide, acuminate at apex, acute to obtuse or sometimes rounded at base, with 10–13 pairs of lateral nerves, sparsely hairy on both surfaces or more rarely glabrescent; petioles 0.8–5.5 cm. long; stipules ovate, 6–12 mm. long, 4–9 mm. wide, acute at apex or sometimes shortly bilobed, hairy outside, glabrous within, reflexing. Fruit narrowly ellipsoid to cylindrical, 2–2.9 cm. long, 0.7–0.9 cm. wide, crowned by persistent calyx-lobes, very sparsely hairy. description: Bulbous geophyte, ± 150 mm tall. Leaves 2 or 3(4), dry at flowering, spreading, narrowly strap-shaped, firm, fleshy and elliptical in cross section, smooth, slightly sticky, curved towards apex. Flowers funnel-shaped, in a spreading cluster, pale pink and translucent, scape sticky, filaments thick and the inner surface papillose at base. Bulb solitary or occasionally forming bulblets, ovoidal, 15-40 mm diam., covered by several thick dry tan-coloured, cartilaginous tunics; neck up to 80 mm long. Leaves absent at anthesis, (1-)2-3(-4), suberect to spreading, lorate, up to 150 x 2.5-5.0 mm, firm, fleshy, compressed-terete in cross section, glabrous, occasionally somewhat sticky, shiny green, curved or twisted distally; subterranean cataphyll and prophyll lacking. Inflorescence laxly or densely hemispherical, 25-60 mm across; scape 25-70 mm long, 1.5-3.0 mm diam., more or less sticky, green to wine red, breaking off at the base in fruit; spathe valves lanceolate, 13-32 x 3-6 mm; bracteoles up to 3 mm long. Flowers 6-17, spreading, funnel-shaped, pale pink and somewhat hyaline, turning light brown with age, scentless; pedicels straight, 19-22 mm long, trigonous, green to pink, ultimately wine-red. Tepals adnate to the stamens and extended into a distinct tube 0.5-1.8 mm long, slightly spreading above, oblanceolate, 4.5-6.5 x 1-1.5 mm. Stamens well exserted, proximally adpressed to the style for up to 2 mm, otherwise slightly spreading; filaments 7-11 mm long, basally connate forming a tube up to 0.5 mm above the perigone throat, otherwise free, papillose adaxially for approximately 2 mm above the throat and raised to form a short inwardly-curved hook, smooth and subulate above; anthers dorsifixed, about 1.5 mm long before opening, dark maroon; pollen cream-coloured. Ovary usually with 1 ovule per locule. Style up to 15 mm long, equalling the stamens, slender throughout, with nectar collecting in a pool around the base; stigma very shortly trifid. Seeds about 2.5 mm diam. Flowering late February until the end of March.

description: Branches of partial inflorescence and bases of bracteoles incrassate and lignescent in fruit, the whole forming a soft, silky-hairy, burr-like unit. Bracteoles of the partial inflorescences broadly cordate-ovate, 5–7 mm. long, ciliate or pilose, hyaline with the darker midrib excurrent in a fine arista up to 1.5 mm. long; bracteoles of secondary triads deltoid-ovate, c. 7–9 mm. long, pilose along the midrib with a rigid arista; bracteoles of the sterile flowers narrower, densely pilose along the midrib with multicellular hairs, the arista very long (almost as long as the lamina), more solid in fruit and finally up to c. 12 mm. long. Fruit compressed-ovoid, c. 3 mm. long, apex concave with a distinct raised rim; seed brown, smooth and shining, c. 2 mm. long, finely reticulate. Sterile flowers of 2 rapidly developing linear, bracteoliform processes densely clothed with long white hairs. Inflorescence considerably lengthening in fruit, (1.5) 2.5–16 × 1.5 × 2.5 (3) cm., axis more or less densely furnished with flexuose whitish hairs, formed of numerous densely set partial inflorescences comprising three or four fertile flowers, two central and solitary and the others subtended by a modified sterile flower on each side; partial inflorescences soon falling in fruit, the persistent bracts strongly deflexed. Bracts broadly ovate, 4.5–5.5 mm. long, furnished with appressed white hairs, rather abruptly acuminate, finely aristate with the long-excurrent midrib. Stem and branches quadrangular, thinly to more or less densely upwardly-appressed pilose. Leaves narrowly lanceolate to broadly elliptic or ovate, subacute to acuminate, those of the main stem and large branches 2.5–10 × 0.8–4.5 cm., moderately white pilose on both surfaces or more densely so below, cuneate or attenuate at the base into a distinct, 3–15 mm. long petiole; superior leaves of branches smaller, generally sessile. description: Because of the weakly developed root system and the absence of woodiness at the base of the stem, N. deflexa could easily be mistaken for an annual, and in most situations (e.g. the type locality), it almost certainly behaves as one. However, given adequate water and nutrients, plants are capable of surviving the hot, dry summer period of the western Cape (at least in cultivation). This is in contrast to the situation for most, if not all, spring-flowering annual Nemesia species. They do not survive the high temperatures associated with summer drought even when supplied with ample water and nutrients. It is not known whether plants of Nemesia deflexa ever survive for a full year or more in the natural environment. It is probable that in most situations, they survive the dry season solely in the form of seed which is produced in fairly large amounts. The seeds germinate readily as soon as they are shed if sufficient moisture is present.

description: An erect slender annual, ranging up to 1 ft. in height, unbranched or branched from the base and forming a rather compact plant, the lower branches developing later. Corolla gaping or ringent, not closed or personate as is usual in Nemesia; rich terra-cotta red changing to a dull grey purple, giving a lovely range of shades in a plant as the flowers develop and fade, the under-surface veined with a deeper colour; on the palate a conspicuous boss densely covered with yellow hairs adds much to the attractiveness of the flower. description: Nemesia suaveolens is easily recognized by its yellow and magenta flowers with a ± straight spur and a prominent yellow rectangular spot (nectar guide) at the base of the upper corolla lip. It is most closely related to N. euryceras, but differs from that species by having a lower lip that is yellow rather than white with pale violet margins, an upper lip with a conspicuous yellow rectangular patch, just above the corolla opening, a spur that is ± equal to the length of the lower lip, not half the length of the lower lip, and a hypochile that is yellow rather than dark violet. Nemesia suaveolens often grows in close proximity to N. karroensis Bond and has been confused with that species. It is similar in coloration to N. karroensis, especially when both are pressed and dried, but differs in having a short, straight, downwardly oriented spur instead of a long (8.9-12.3 mm), backwardly projecting one that is usually strongly recurved in its distal half.
